lessons.title: The Anvil: Parts and Proper Use
lessons.body:
The anvil is the heart of your forge. In Africa, you can find new anvils from suppliers in Nairobi, Lagos, or Johannesburg, but many smiths use a heavy piece of railway line or a solid block of scrap steel. A good anvil weighs between 50 kg and 150 kg. It must sit on a sturdy baseâa thick wooden stump buried in the ground works well. The main parts are the face (the flat top), the horn (the pointed end), the heel (the square end), the step (a lower flat area near the horn), and the hardy hole (a square hole for tools) and pritchel hole (a round hole for punching).

When you work, the anvil should be at knuckle height when you stand straight. This saves your back and gives you full swing. Secure the anvil so it does not bounce. You can chain it to the stump or use metal straps. The face must be smooth but not polishedâa slight texture helps grip the hot metal. Never hammer on the face when it is cold, and never use the anvil as a welding table without protecting it.

Use the horn for bending curves. The step is for cutting with a chisel, so you don't damage the main face. The hardy hole holds tools like the hardy cutter. The pritchel hole is for punching holesâthe punch goes through the metal and into the hole. Keep the face clean; wipe off scale and rust with a wire brush. A light oil rub once a week prevents rust in humid climates. If the edges are chipped, grind them smooth with an angle grinder, but keep a small radius on the edges for drawing out metal without cutting it.

A common mistake is to hammer directly on the anvil without a workpiece. That dents the face and can chip it. Always have hot metal between your hammer and the anvil. Also, never strike the anvil with a hardened hammerâit can shatter. With proper care, a good anvil will last for generations.

lessons.title: Hammers: Types, Weights, and Handling
lessons.body:
As a blacksmith, your hammer is your main tool. You need at least two: a heavy hammer for drawing out metal (around 1.5 to 2 kg or 3â4 lb) and a lighter one for finishing and detail work (around 0.5 to 1 kg or 1â2 lb). In Africa, you can buy blacksmith hammers from industrial suppliers or make your own from car axles or leaf springs. The head should be hardened but not brittle. The handle should be hickory or local hardwood like mukwa or irokoâstraight-grained and free of knots. Fit the handle through the eye and wedge it tight with a metal wedge and a wooden wedge at right angles. The handle length should be about 30â35 cm, and the end should be slightly flared so it doesn't slip out of your hand.

Grip the hammer near the end of the handle, not close to the head. This gives you more leverage and power. Your thumb should wrap around the handle, not rest on top. When you swing, use your whole arm, not just your wrist. Let the hammer do the workâraise it and let it fall with gravity. For heavy drawing out, use the flat face. For rounding, use the ball peen. For texturing, you can use a cross peen or a straight peen. Always strike the metal flat; if you strike at an angle, you will leave marks and waste energy.

Keep your hammer face smooth and slightly domed. If it gets mushroomed, grind off the mushroomed edges immediatelyâthey can break off and injure you. Never use a hammer with a loose head. Check the wedges regularly and tighten them if needed. Store hammers hanging on a rack or lying flat on a shelf, not on the floor where they can get damaged or cause a trip hazard. A well-maintained hammer will give you years of service.

lessons.title: Tongs: Selecting and Using the Right Pair
lessons.body:
Tongs are your hands in the forge. They hold hot metal so you can hammer, twist, or cut it. You need several pairs because different jobs require different jaws. The most common types are flat-jaw tongs for holding flat bar, box-jaw tongs for square or round stock, and pick-up tongs for small pieces. In Africa, you can buy tongs from blacksmith suppliers or make your own from mild steel. A good pair of tongs is made from 10â12 mm round or square bar, with jaws that fit the stock you are working with. The reins (handles) should be long enough to keep your hands away from the heatâat least 40 cm. The joint should be a rivet or a bolt that allows smooth opening and closing.

When selecting tongs, match the jaw shape to the workpiece. For flat bar, use flat jaws that grip the sides. For round bar, use box jaws or V-jaws that hold the curve. The jaws should close completely without gaps. If they don't, heat them and adjust with a hammer. The reins should be comfortable to hold; you can curve them slightly outward for better grip. Always hold the tongs with the workpiece centered in the jaws, not at the tip, to avoid dropping it.

Never use tongs to hold cold metal for heavy hammeringâthey can slip. For heavy work, use a tong with a longer handle and a tighter grip. Keep the joint lubricated with a drop of oil. If the jaws get too hot, cool them in waterâbut don't quench hot tongs in water if they are made of high-carbon steel, as they may crack. Instead, let them air cool. Store tongs hanging on a rack or lying flat. A good pair of tongs will last for many years if you don't use them as a hammer or pry bar.

lessons.title: Hardies, Swages, and Fullers
lessons.body:
Hardies, swages, and fullers are tools that fit into the hardy hole or are held by hand. The hardy is a chisel-like tool that fits in the anvil's hardy hole. It is used for cutting hot metal. You place the hot metal on the hardy and strike it with a hammer. The hardy should be made of high-carbon steel and hardened. It should fit snugly in the hole but be easy to remove. Keep the cutting edge sharp with a file or grinder. Never cut cold metal with a hardyâit will chip. Also, never leave a hardy in the anvil when not in use; it can trip you or get damaged.

Swages are used to shape metal into curves or rounds. A top swage is held by a handle and struck with a hammer; a bottom swage fits in the hardy hole. Together they form a round or oval shape. For example, to make a round bar from square stock, you use a swage with a half-round groove. Swages come in different sizes. In Africa, you can make your own swages by grinding grooves into a block of steel. Fullers are similar but have a rounded, convex face. They are used to draw out metal quickly or to make grooves. A top fuller is held by a handle; a bottom fuller fits in the hardy hole. You strike the top fuller to push metal into the bottom fuller, thinning and spreading it.

When using these tools, always work with hot metalâat least a bright orange heat. Strike squarely and evenly. Keep the tools clean and free of scale. Store them in a rack or box, not on the floor. A hardy that is too loose can bounce out and injure you, so check the fit regularly. If it's too loose, you can shim it with a piece of sheet metal. With practice, these tools will speed up your work and improve the quality of your forgings.

lessons.title: Measuring and Marking Tools
lessons.body:
Accurate measuring and marking are essential for making consistent products. You need a steel rule or tape measure (at least 30 cm), a try square, a scriber or a soapstone marker, and a center punch. In Africa, you can find these at hardware stores or market stalls. A steel rule is best for precise work; a tape measure is fine for longer lengths. The try square checks 90-degree angles and marks lines across bars. A scriber is a sharp-pointed steel rod for scratching lines on metal. Soapstone is a natural stone that leaves a white mark on hot or cold metalâit's cheap and easy to find. A center punch is a pointed tool you strike with a hammer to make a small dent, which guides a drill bit.

Before you cut or bend, mark your workpiece clearly. Use soapstone on hot metalâit won't burn off like paint. For cold metal, use a scriber or a permanent marker. Measure twice, mark once. When marking, hold the rule or square firmly against the metal. For a square line, place the try square against the edge and scribe along the blade. For a center line, measure from both edges and mark the midpoint. Use a center punch to mark hole locations. Strike it once with a hammer to make a dent. This prevents the drill from wandering.

Keep your measuring tools clean and dry. Store them in a box or pouch, not loose in a toolbox where they can get bent or rusty. A steel rule can get damaged if used as a scraper or pry bar. Check your try square regularly for squarenessâif it's out, your work will be out. A simple test is to mark a line, flip the square, and mark again; if the lines don't match, the square is off. Replace or adjust it. Good measuring habits save time and material.

lessons.title: Tool Maintenance and Storage
lessons.body:
Your tools are an investment. Proper maintenance and storage will keep them working safely and last for years. At the end of each day, wipe down all tools with an oily rag to prevent rust. In humid African climates, rust can appear overnight. Use any light oilâengine oil, coconut oil, or even used cooking oil works in a pinch. For the anvil, wire-brush the face and oil it. For hammers and tongs, check for cracks, loose handles, or mushroomed heads. Grind off any mushrooming immediately. For hardies and swages, check the edges and grind them sharp if needed. Keep the hardy hole clean of scale and debris.

Store tools in a dry place. A wooden box or a rack on the wall is ideal. Hang tongs and hammers on pegs so they don't touch the floor. Keep the anvil on its stump, not on the ground where it can rust. If you have a dirt floor, place a wooden pallet or a concrete slab under your work area to reduce moisture. Never store tools in a damp corner or near a forge that is not in useâcondensation can form. For long-term storage, coat tools with grease or wrap them in oiled cloth.

Schedule a weekly maintenance check. Tighten hammer wedges, oil tong joints, and check the anvil for chips. Replace worn handles. A loose hammer head is dangerousâfix it before you use it again. Keep a file and a grinder handy for touch-ups. Teach yourself to inspect tools before each use: look for cracks, loose parts, or damage. If a tool is unsafe, repair it or discard it. Don't take chances. A well-maintained toolkit is the mark of a professional blacksmith.

quiz.q: What is the main part of the anvil used for bending curves?
quiz.explanation: The horn is the pointed end used for bending curves.

quiz.q: What is the hardy hole used for?
options: B) Holding tools like the hardy cutter
quiz.explanation: The hardy hole is a square hole that holds tools such as the hardy cutter.

quiz.q: At what height should the anvil be set?
quiz.explanation: The anvil should be at knuckle height to save your back and give full swing.

quiz.q: What should you never do on the anvil's face?
quiz.explanation: Hammering cold metal can damage the anvil face.

quiz.q: What is the pritchel hole used for?
quiz.explanation: The pritchel hole is a round hole used for punching holes.

quiz.q: What is the recommended weight for a heavy drawing hammer?
quiz.explanation: A heavy hammer for drawing out metal is typically 1.5 to 2 kg.

quiz.q: How should you grip a hammer?
options: C) Near the end of the handle
quiz.explanation: Gripping near the end gives more leverage and power.

quiz.q: What should you do if a hammer head is mushroomed?
options: B) Grind off the mushroomed edges
quiz.explanation: Mushroomed edges can break off and injure you, so grind them off.

quiz.q: What type of wood is recommended for a hammer handle?
quiz.explanation: Hickory or local hardwood like mukwa or iroko is strong and shock-absorbing.

quiz.q: How should you swing a hammer?
quiz.explanation: Using your whole arm gives more power and control.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of tongs?
quiz.explanation: Tongs are used to hold hot metal safely.

quiz.q: Which type of tongs is best for holding flat bar?
quiz.explanation: Flat-jaw tongs grip the sides of flat bar.

quiz.q: What is the recommended length for tong reins?
quiz.explanation: Long reins keep your hands away from the heat.

quiz.q: How should you hold the workpiece in the tongs?
options: A) At the tip of the jaws
quiz.explanation: Centering the workpiece prevents it from slipping.

quiz.q: What should you do if tong jaws get too hot?
quiz.explanation: Quenching high-carbon steel tongs can cause cracking; air cooling is safer.

quiz.q: What is a hardy used for?
quiz.explanation: The hardy is a chisel-like tool for cutting hot metal.

quiz.q: Where does a bottom swage fit?
quiz.explanation: A bottom swage fits in the hardy hole.

quiz.q: What is a fuller used for?
quiz.explanation: Fullers are used to draw out metal or make grooves.

quiz.q: What heat should metal be at when using a hardy?
quiz.explanation: Hot metal at bright orange is easier to cut and won't damage the hardy.

quiz.q: How should you store hardies and swages?
options: B) In a rack or box
quiz.explanation: Storing in a rack or box prevents damage and loss.

quiz.q: What is a scriber used for?
quiz.explanation: A scriber is a sharp-pointed tool for scratching lines on metal.

quiz.q: What is soapstone used for?
quiz.explanation: Soapstone leaves a white mark on hot or cold metal.

quiz.q: What is a center punch used for?
options: A) Making a dent for drilling
quiz.explanation: A center punch makes a small dent to guide a drill bit.

quiz.q: How should you check a try square for squareness?
options: A) Mark a line, flip, mark again
D) Tap it on the anvil
quiz.explanation: If the lines don't match after flipping, the square is off.

quiz.q: Why should you measure twice and mark once?
quiz.explanation: Double-checking measurements prevents costly errors.

quiz.q: What should you do to tools at the end of each day?
quiz.explanation: Wiping with an oily rag prevents rust.

quiz.q: Where should you store tools?
options: C) In a dry place on a rack or box
quiz.explanation: A dry place prevents rust and damage.

quiz.q: How often should you do a maintenance check on tools?
quiz.explanation: A weekly check helps catch issues before they become dangerous.

quiz.q: What should you do with a loose hammer head?
quiz.explanation: A loose hammer head is dangerous and must be fixed.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid quenching high-carbon steel tongs in water?
quiz.explanation: Quenching can cause high-carbon steel to crack.
